articles.title: Access-to-killing relay by wavelength-division Janus nanomotors for biofilm phototherapy.
articles.abstract: Biofilm phototherapy is constrained by therapeutic reach, as light-triggered damage is often concentrated near accessible regions while bacteria remain protected within the extracellular matrix. Here we report wavelength-division Janus nanomotors for access-gated biofilm phototherapy, in which asymmetric interfacial energy conversion and wavelength-resolved activation couple active transport with antibacterial action. articles.title: Evaluation of Experimental Nanocomposite-Based Solution and Dentifrice for Reducing Dental Erosive Wear.
articles.abstract: To assess the in vitro effect of experimental solution and dentifrice on the progression of erosive tooth wear. Bovine enamel (n = 40) and root dentin (n = 40) specimens were pre-eroded (0.3% HCl; pH 1.2; 5 min) and randomized into 4 groups (n = 10, per group): experimental solution based on mesoporous silica containing calcium and fluoride (MSCaNaF); experimental dentifrice based on magnesium and fluoride (MgF2) and negative (water, Milli-Q®) and positive (stannous-containing dentifrice, Elmex®) controls. After half-covering, the specimens were submitted to a second erosive challenge for 5 days (100 μL; 1min; 3×/day). Differences in volumetric roughness (Sa) and tooth structure loss (TSL) by use of 3D noncontact optical profilometry were evaluated. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed. The data were analyzed by Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney, and Wilcoxon tests (α=0.05). The intra-group evaluation of Sa showed that all groups differed from the initial condition. For Sa, in relation to enamel and dentin, all experimental groups showed a difference in roughness compared with the negative control (p < 0.05). TSL analysis revealed that the MSCaNaF, MgF2, and positive control groups were similar (p>0.05) and more effective compared to the negative control (p<0.05). In the SEM images, the negative control presented the worst loss of dental structure, with more porous enamel. The dentine surface topography pattern showed partially or totally occluded dentinal tubules after treatments, except in the negative control group. The new products based on MSCaNaF and MgF2 are effective in controlling the progression of dental erosion, similar to commercial products.

articles.title: Rapid Pain Reduction and Wound Closure Following Treatment With an Amorphous Silica-Based Fiber Wound Matrix in Partial-Thickness Thermal Burns: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Partial-thickness thermal burns can cause substantial pain and require effective wound management to support re-epithelialization. A 30-year-old man sustained 3%-4% total body surface area partial-thickness burns of the left hand, forearm, elbow, and abdomen following a gasoline-accelerated brush fire. Despite emergency debridement, dressings, and multimodal analgesia, pain remained 6-10/10. Approximately two days after injury, an amorphous silica-based fiber (SBF) wound matrix was applied to the open wounds, while a silica-based cream (SBC) was applied to surrounding intact skin. At initial SBF/SBC treatment, patient-reported pain decreased from 7/10 to 0/10 on a 0-10 numerical rating scale (NRS), with substantial relief reported within approximately 5-10 minutes. Across 12 paired assessments, mean pain decreased from 2.46/10 before treatment to 1.17/10 afterward. Serial planimetry demonstrated progressive wound closure with complete measured closure by Day 10, with sustained epithelial coverage and minimal scarring at Day 63. Because partial-thickness burns may spontaneously re-epithelialize, and this represents a single uncontrolled case with prior and concomitant treatment, causality cannot be established. The observed temporal pain response and wound-healing trajectory support prospective controlled evaluation using standardized pain, analgesic-use, epithelialization, functional, and safety endpoints.

articles.title: Multifunctional nanocomposite with stage-responsive behavior for wound healing.
articles.abstract: Chronic wounds, particularly refractory diabetic ulcers, typically fail to heal due to a self-perpetuating inflammatory state driven by persistent bacterial infection, severe oxidative stress, and impaired microvascular regeneration. Conventional static dressings cannot accommodate the spatiotemporal, multiphase complexity of tissue repair. Here, a stage-responsive hierarchical nanocomposite (SNF@GQDs@Arg) was engineered by covalently anchoring graphene quantum dots (GQDs) onto radially porous silica nanoflowers (SNF), followed by surface adsorption of L-arginine (L-Arg). The resulting platform coordinates wound repair through an integrated tripartite-physical, catalytic, and metabolic-cascade. articles.title: Pickering Emulsions with Long-Term Stability from Ultrafine Amphiphilic Benzyl-Modified Silica Nanoparticles.
articles.abstract: Pickering emulsions offer superior stability and eco-friendly properties across multiple industries due to solid particle stabilization at oil-water interfaces. However, the design and synthesis of ultrafine nanoparticles capable of stabilizing Pickering emulsions have always been a challenging problem. Herein, ultrafine silica nanoparticles which have a diameter of 20-30 nm, were prepared based on a microemulsion method. The ultrafine silica nanoparticles have excellent dispersion properties in water. The benzyl-modified amphiphilic silica nanoparticles were synthesized by grafting benzyl groups onto the nanoparticle surface using the Pickering emulsion template method after modification with 3-[2-(2-aminoethylamino)ethylamino]propyl-trimethoxysilane. The benzyl-modified silica nanoparticles have excellent interfacial activity, with a three-phase contact angle close to 90°, and can reduce the interfacial tension of the kerosene/water system. The resulting Pickering emulsions stabilized by benzyl-modified silica nanoparticles have excellent long-term stability (stable for at least 200 days). Additionally, benzyl-modified silica nanoparticles can also be used as Pickering emulsifiers for soybean oil, sunflower oil, n-hexadecane, and mineral oil, and they exhibit potential application scenarios in fields such as the food and cosmetics industry, catalytic synthesis, and sustained drug release.

articles.title: Advancing nanomaterials for treatment of eye diseases: a review.
articles.abstract: Ocular diseases involving both the anterior and posterior segments-such as dry eye disease, keratitis, glaucoma, cataracts, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and ocular tumors-remain major contributors to global visual impairment. Conventional topical and systemic therapies are limited by rapid clearance, restricted penetration across ocular barriers, and poor bioavailability, particularly for posterior-segment targets. Nanotechnology has introduced a transformative therapeutic paradigm by enabling controlled pharmacokinetics, enhanced tissue penetration, and site-specific delivery. A wide range of engineered nanomaterials-including polymeric nanoparticles, lipid-based carriers, dendrimers, metallic and metal-oxide nanoparticles, mesoporous silica systems, cerium oxide nanozymes, carbon quantum dots, nanogels, and electrospun nanofibers-has demonstrated improved drug loading, sustained release, ocular surface retention, and compatibility with biologics and gene-based agents. Emerging minimally invasive platforms, such as 4D printed smart scaffolds, dissolving microneedles and magnetically driven microrobots, further enable precise transscleral or intravitreal delivery, active navigation through the vitreous, and targeted interaction with retinal lesions. Parallel clinical advances, including FDA-approved nanoformulations and ongoing trials, confirm the translational potential of these technologies. Plus, artificial intelligence now accelerates both ophthalmic diagnosis and nanocarrier design, enabling predictive modeling of nano-bio interactions, personalized delivery strategies, and real-time disease assessment. This review integrates current advances in nanomaterial engineering and AI-guided innovation, outlining their convergent roles in shaping next-generation precision therapeutics for vision preservation and restoration.

articles.title: Solid-phase extraction of flavonoids: A comprehensive review and comparative benchmarking of sorbent classes.
articles.abstract: Flavonoids are polyphenol-type secondary metabolites that plants do not synthesize for primary growth and development, but rather produce mostly for defense or for pigmentation in flowers. These substances are compounds with strong antioxidant activity that are used in the manufacture of medicines, cosmetic creams, and food supplements. Due to their low concentration in samples and the presence of interfering substances in the sample matrix, their analysis is difficult. To solve this problem, sample clean-up and concentration are necessary, for which various methods, including the solid-phase extraction (SPE) method, are used. In this method, sorbents play a fundamental role and act as selective extraction phases for matrix clean-up and analyte enrichment. In this review article, six classes of SPE sorbents that have been used so far for the extraction of flavonoids-porous frameworks (MOFs/COFs), carbon-based nanomaterials (graphene, CNTs), molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs), macroporous resins, functionalized silica and metal oxides, and bio-based polymer composites (such as chitosan)-have been reviewed. In this review, the structural features of the sorbent (such as surface area, pore size, and functional groups) and the mechanisms affecting adsorption, including π-π interactions, hydrogen bonds, and electrostatic forces, have been evaluated. Recovery efficiency, chemical stability, regenerability (reusability), selectivity, and environmental compatibility have been investigated. This review provides a perspective on the effects of sample matrix and enrichment parameters and helps researchers identify promising SPE platforms for modern, high-throughput analysis of flavonoids.

articles.title: Design of silica-core gold-shell nanoparticles for photothermal breast tumor therapy: a two-arm comparison of surface cooling with nanoparticle self-attenuation.
articles.abstract: We assemble a three-layer forward model for gold nanoshell photothermal therapy, core-shell Mie absorption, Pennes bioheat transport, and an Arrhenius thermal dose, each benchmarked against an external reference, and use it to maximize necrosis depth subject to a skin-temperature cap. The design variables are core radius, shell thickness, and irradiance at 808 nm; number density is derived per geometry from a fixed delivered gold mass anchored to a measured in vivo loading. The Beer-Lambert source deposits heat from both nanoparticle and native tissue absorption and includes self-attenuation, so the deposition shape depends on the design; at fixed geometry, the rise is exact in the source amplitude, so envelope inversion pins the safety cap in closed form. The search is a two-arm comparison differing onlyin the skin boundary condition. For near-surface loading under a common skin-temperature constraint, the no-cooling control admits no viable therapy (necrosis 0), while contact cooling reaches 15.6 mm at a 15 ◦C skin surface. As a secondary, boundary-dependent observation, at each arm's own safety limit the cooled optimum is 3.6 mm deeper than a control that reaches depth only by heating the skin to about 83 ◦C. The control becomes viable only once a nanoparticle-free skin cap exceeds about 5.6 mm, its surface still at the 45 ◦C cap; cooling remains the deeper arm at every cap thickness tested. Methodologically, omitting self-attenuation makes the necrosis objective appear geometry-independent, whereas resolving it makes particle geometry a design lever comparable to cooling, though the favored geometry is a model-dependent trend rather than a located optimum. The headline depths derive from a homogeneous constant-perfusion model with a ubiquitous nanoparticle distribution rather than a tumor-localized one; the cap sweep relaxes that distribution but not the constant perfusion. All depths are theoretical upper bounds, not clinical predictions.

articles.title: Physically retained charge-dense interfaces enhance piezoionic sensing under physiologically relevant ionic conditions.
articles.abstract: Piezoionic hydrogels convert mechanical deformation into ionic signals through pressure-driven ion migration, offering self-powered operation and mechanical compliance suitable for integration with biological tissues. However, conventional piezoionic systems rely on the redistribution of freely mobile ions, making their output strongly dependent on maintaining an optimized internal electrolyte composition and potentially attenuated under physiologically relevant ionic conditions. Here, we report a piezoionic hydrogel designed to retain charge-dense interfaces within a hydrated polymer network. Polyamine-looped silica (PLS) nanoparticles are retained within a polyacrylamide (PAM) scaffold with no detectable particle loss under the tested hydration conditions, while their surface-loop architecture is proposed to promote topological interpenetration with the surrounding polymer network. The positively charged interfaces are proposed to favor the local association of anionic species, thereby contributing to asymmetric ion redistribution during compression. Comparisons with bare silica and amine-functionalized silica (AFS) nanoparticles indicate that the enhanced response is associated with both the charge characteristics and retention of the PLS-containing interfaces. The PLS-containing architecture maintains mechanical recoverability over the tested 20 compression cycles and produces reproducible piezoionic responses over 100 cycles.
